source_balance_context.text: Epilepsy is a group of neurological diseases characterized by susceptibility to recurrent seizures. Antiseizure medications (ASMs) are the mainstay of treatment, but many antiseizure medications with variable safety profiles have been approved for use. For women with epilepsy in their childbearing years, the safety profile is important for them and their unborn children, because treatment is often required to protect them from seizures during pregnancy and lactation. Since no large randomized controlled trials have investigated safety in this subgroup of people with epilepsy, pregnancy registries, cohort and case-control studies from population registries, and a few large prospective cohort studies have played an important role. Valproate, in monotherapy and polytherapy, has been associated with elevated risk of major congenital malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders in children born to mothers who took it. Topiramate and phenobarbital are also associated with elevated risks of congenital malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders, though the risks are lower than those of valproate. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam are relatively safe. Insufficient data exist to reach strong conclusions about the newest antiseizure medications such as eslicarbazepine, perampanel, brivaracetam, cannabidiol, and cenobamate. Besides antiseizure medications, other treatments such as vagal nerve stimulation, responsive neurostimulation, and deep brain stimulation are likely safe. In general, breastfeeding does not appear to add any additional long term risks to the child. Creative ways of optimizing registry enrollment and data collection are needed to enhance patient safety.

source_balance_context.text: There is still limited knowledge about alterations of blood concentrations of psychotropic drugs during pregnancy, the transfer of psychotropic drugs into breastmilk and the effects on exposed children. We investigated changes in concentrations of psychopharmacological medication during pregnancy and lactation in serum and breastmilk at different time points in a naturalistic sample of 60 mothers and observed the development of the exposed children in the first 12 months. We found a decrease in serum concentrations from the first to the second trimester of amitriptyline, duloxetine, escitalopram, quetiapine and sertraline. Citalopram stayed rather stable during pregnancy, sertraline levels interestingly increased again from the second to the third trimester. High concentration-by-dose ratios in breastmilk were found for venlafaxine as well as lamotrigine, low for quetiapine and clomipramine. Similarly, clomipramine and quetiapine showed low milk/serum-penetration ratios. Regarding the birth outcome measures in children, we found no significant differences between in utero exposed compared to nonexposed newborns. There were no significant differences in the development in the first 12 months. Psychotropic medication in the peripartum needs a balancing of risks and benefits and a continuous therapeutic drug monitoring can be a guidance for clinicians to monitor drug alteration patterns, which are likely to occur due to physiological pregnancy-associated changes in pharmacokinetics. Accordingly, therapeutic drug monitoring can optimize a medication in pregnancy and lactation with the lowest effective dose.

source_balance_context.text: Seizure disorders are the most frequent major neurologic complication in pregnancy, affecting 0.3% to 0.8% of all gestations. Women of childbearing age with epilepsy require special care related to pregnancy. This article provides up-to-date information to guide practitioners in the management of epilepsy in pregnancy. Ongoing multicenter pregnancy registries and studies continue to provide important information on issues related to pregnancy in women with epilepsy. Valproate poses a special risk for malformations and cognitive/behavioral impairments. A few antiseizure medications pose low risks (eg, lamotrigine, levetiracetam), but the risks for many antiseizure medications remain uncertain. Although pregnancy rates differ, a prospective study found no difference in fertility rates between women with epilepsy who were attempting to get pregnant and healthy controls. During pregnancy, folic acid supplementation is important, and a dose greater than 400 mcg/d during early pregnancy (ie, first 12 weeks) is associated with better neurodevelopmental outcome in children of women with epilepsy. Breastfeeding is not harmful and should be encouraged in women with epilepsy even when they are on antiseizure medication treatment. Women with epilepsy should be counseled early and regularly about reproductive health. Practitioners should discuss the risks of various obstetric complications; potential anatomic teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental dysfunction related to fetal antiseizure medication exposure; and a plan of care during pregnancy, delivery, and postpartum. Women with epilepsy should also be reassured that the majority of pregnancies are uneventful.

source_balance_context.text: The management of epilepsy during pregnancy involves optimizing seizure control for the mother, while ensuring the best outcome for the developing fetus. Preconception counseling regarding contraception, folic acid, and antiseizure medications (ASMs) will maximize positive outcomes. Folic acid supplementation is recommended to decrease risk of neural tube defects, similar to the general population, and has been associated with improved cognitive outcomes and decreased risk of autistic traits in offspring. Efforts should be made to optimize the ASM regimen before pregnancy to the fewest number of ASMs, lowest effective doses, with avoidance of more teratogenic agents such as valproic acid. Valproic acid is associated with the highest increased risk of major congenital malformations, as well as reduced cognitive outcomes and neurodevelopmental disorders. Decreasing or changing ASMs during pregnancy should be done with caution, as convulsive seizures have been associated with adverse fetal outcomes including cognitive impairment. Physiologic changes during pregnancy affect ASM levels and in turn, risk for seizures, necessitating frequent monitoring of ASM serum concentrations. Mothers should also be counseled postpartum about how the benefits of breastfeeding outweigh the transmission of medication into breast milk. Communication between providers (obstetrics and neurology) and pregnant women with epilepsy is essential.

answer:
## Lamotrigine pregnancy evidence

**Evidence scope:** Lamotrigine identity was verified. The retrieved evidence consists of one selected DailyMed product label plus a bounded PubMed search; it is not a systematic review. The DailyMed label is for one product/formulation, with effective date **October 12, 2026** and publication date **November 9, 2026**. Its pregnancy text was truncated in one field, although the structured PLLR 8.1 sections were returned. DailyMed states that in-use labeling may differ from the latest FDA-approved labeling. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Maternal effects and underlying disease

The label states that most lamotrigine pregnancy data come from women with **epilepsy**. It separately describes pregnancy-associated risks reported with epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-drug exposure, including preeclampsia, preterm labor, hemorrhage, placental abruption, poor fetal growth, prematurity, fetal death, and maternal mortality. These are presented as **underlying-disease and treatment-context risks**, not as lamotrigine-specific adverse effects. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label also reports that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, with reports of decreased concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. This is source labeling for clinician discussion, not an individualized medication plan. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

A 2023 review of epilepsy in pregnancy and lactation states that pregnancy safety evidence in this population relies substantially on pregnancy registries, cohort studies, case-control studies, and prospective cohorts because large randomized safety trials have not been conducted. The source population is **pregnant women with epilepsy and lactation**, and the publication type is **review**. [S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684052/)

### Fetal or infant exposure

No numeric human fetal concentration was retrieved.

A 2023 study of **60 mothers**, with source populations including **pregnancy, lactation, neonates, and children**, measured psychotropic-medication concentrations in serum and breastmilk at multiple time points and followed exposed children during the first 12 months. Its abstract reports a high breastmilk concentration-to-dose ratio for lamotrigine, but does not provide a lamotrigine-specific milk concentration, fetal concentration, or infant-level concentration in the retrieved text. The study design label was not stated in the returned abstract metadata. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

The label reports animal findings, including decreased fetal folate concentrations in rats and developmental findings in animals. These are **animal data**, not measured human fetal exposure. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Observed fetal and infant outcomes

For **lamotrigine monotherapy during the first trimester**, the label reports:

- International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.2%** of **1,558** exposed infants; 95% CI **1.6%–3.1%**.
- NAAED Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.0%** of **1,562** exposed infants.
- EURAP registry: major birth defects in **2.9%** of **2,514** exposures; 95% CI **2.3%–3.7%**.

The label states that the frequency of major congenital malformations was similar to general-population estimates. The underlying registry populations and comparator methods differ, so these figures should not be treated as a single pooled estimate. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

**Isolated oral clefts:** The NAAED Pregnancy Registry reported oral clefts in **3.2 per 1,000** among **2,200** infants exposed early in pregnancy; 95% CI **1.4–6.3**, described in the label as a threefold increase versus unexposed healthy controls. The label states that this finding was not observed in other large international pregnancy registries. A European case-control study reported an adjusted odds ratio of **1.45**; 95% CI **0.8–2.63**. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age outcomes, and neurodevelopmental delay. It also states that differences in outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limit the conclusions. The retrieved extract does not establish a lamotrigine-specific effect estimate for each of these outcomes. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The 60-mother naturalistic study reported no significant differences in birth outcomes between its in-utero-exposed and nonexposed newborn groups and no significant differences in development during the first 12 months. The abstract does not establish the lamotrigine-specific subgroup size or outcome estimates, so this finding should not be generalized to all lamotrigine-exposed pregnancies. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

### FAERS report-only context

For the queried lamotrigine pregnancy-report subset, FAERS returned:

| Reported term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| Foetal exposure during pregnancy | 3,527 |
| Atrial septal defect | 357 |
| Congenital anomaly | 327 |
| Premature baby | 257 |
| Ventricular septal defect | 205 |
| Patent ductus arteriosus | 153 |
| Spina bifida | 143 |
| Hypospadias | 135 |

These are reporting volumes for reports matching the query, not confirmed clinical outcomes, incidence rates, or evidence of causation. The source states that exposure denominators were unavailable and that the results cannot be generalized to all infants or all exposed people. [S2](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22lamotrigine%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S14](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Limitations

- Most label pregnancy data are from women with epilepsy; applicability to bipolar disorder or another indication is not established by the retrieved extract. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
- Registry findings concern specific populations, exposure periods, and comparator groups; they should not be merged into one estimate. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
- Monotherapy findings should not be generalized to polytherapy or unreported co-exposures. The retrieved label data specifically describe monotherapy for the registry percentages. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
- One DailyMed pregnancy field was truncated; missing text is an extraction limitation, not evidence that additional information is absent. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
- Seven requested PubMed records had abstract text retrieved, but the search was bounded and not a complete literature review. [S11](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
- No curated federal pregnancy counterpart to LactMed was identified in this MCP source review; pregnancy findings came from product labeling and primary literature, with non-exhaustive coverage. This is an MCP-generated coverage notice, not a claim that no such resource exists. [S28](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule) [S29](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/)

### Questions for the clinician

1. Which evidence population best matches the underlying condition: epilepsy, bipolar disorder, or another indication?
2. Does the evidence apply to the exact formulation and any co-medications?
3. How should the isolated oral-cleft signal be interpreted given the differing registry findings and comparator groups?
4. Which outcome definitions and gestational periods are most relevant to the research question?
5. What human exposure measurements, if any, are available for the specific pregnancy or infant context?
6. How should the label’s reported pregnancy-related concentration changes be interpreted for the specific clinical context?
7. Would the North American Antiepileptic Drug Pregnancy Registry be relevant to the research discussion? The FDA directory lists it as ongoing, but the directory states that current enrollment should be verified directly. [S27](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries) [S26](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)

The MCP server’s continuity-of-care notice: stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks; such changes belong in discussion with the prescribing clinician.

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

| Evidence axis | Extracted findings | Context-only passages | Gap statements |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Effect on the pregnant or lactating person | 1 extracted candidate passages; source interpretation requires review. | 0 | 1 |
| Measured transfer or exposure to fetus or infant | 3 extracted candidate passages; source interpretation requires review. | 2 | 1 |
| Observed outcomes in fetus or infant | 6 extracted candidate passages; source interpretation requires review. | 4 | 1 |
These are counts of extracted passages, not studies or proven effects. Context-only passages and gap statements are counted separately. Empty rows do not establish absence of evidence elsewhere or safety. This inventory does not replace the cited findings or validate applicability.
